text.en: Imagine a city that was a capital 2,500 years ago and is still a busy city today. Several of the capitals of the early states of India are exactly that. After the Harappan cities faded, India saw a second wave of cities, with states, iron tools and coins. In this chapter we meet the janapadas and mahajanapadas.

After the decline of the Harappan cities some were abandoned, while in others people returned to a rural life. Regional cultures flourished. About 800 to 300 BCE a new phase, often called the Second Urbanisation, began, mainly in the Ganga plains. Interestingly it has continued up to today.
Janapadas were territories of clans or tribes. In time larger and more powerful states emerged, the mahajanapadas, literally great realms. About sixteen are traditionally listed. The most powerful were Magadha in today's Bihar, Kosala in Uttar Pradesh, Vatsa and Avanti in Madhya Pradesh. Most of their ancient capitals remain living cities today, though 2,500 years old. Some were monarchies in which the raja was the highest authority, helped by ministers and an assembly of elders. Others, called ganas or sanghas, were not monarchies. Their assemblies chose the ruler and took major decisions, so their functioning might be called democratic. There is some evidence of warfare between neighbouring mahajanapadas, though we cannot tell how often.
Cities need technology. Iron tools, perfected in several regions from the early 2nd millennium BCE, took a few centuries to become part of everyday life. Iron ploughs cleared forests and increased farm output, and iron weapons strengthened armies. Cities were protected by fortifications, a moat, which is a deep wide ditch around a fort wall, and gateways narrowed to control the movement of people and goods. Shishupalgarh near Bhubaneswar, capital of Kalinga, followed a strict square plan with strong fortifications and broad streets. Coins began to be used. Generally each mahajanapada issued its own coins, but coins from neighbouring regions were used and traded too, even with other parts of the world, which made trade easier. New ideas also rose, such as late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools of thought, as we saw in Grade 6.
A growing city needs many kinds of work: governance, administration, religion, education, trade, town planning, farming, crafts and arts. In an ideal society all these groups complement each other. In India society came to be organised in two ways, varna and jati. A jati often divided further into sub-jatis with their own customs on marriage, rituals or food. The word caste comes from the Portuguese word casta used by travellers in the 16th century CE. In practice people could change occupations, as when a drought forced farmers to migrate to a city and take new work. Inequalities within society exist in many forms, and many people and movements have worked to reduce them.
About the same time the mahajanapadas ceased to exist and new developments, led by Magadha, began to reshape India. The timeline from 1900 BCE to 300 BCE: Harappan Civilisation, Janapadas, Mahajanapadas, Second Urbanisation.

problem.en: Why was iron important for the growth of cities?

text.en: Iron tools are stronger than stone or bronze tools.
Iron ploughs clear forests and raise farm output.
More food supports craftspeople, traders and rulers in cities.

prompt.en: Compare monarchies and ganas or sanghas among the mahajanapadas.

requiredIdeas.en: In monarchies a raja ruled with ministers.
In ganas assemblies chose the ruler.
Both had assemblies of elders or members.

points.en: Janapadas became mahajanapadas, such as Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti.
Iron, coins and fortified capitals drove the Second Urbanisation.
Some states were ruled by assemblies of members.
Society grew complex with many occupations.
